claim: Transcription is an inherently stochastic, noisy, and multi-step process.
source: Transcription is an inherently stochastic, noisy, and multi-step process, in which fluctuations at every step can cause variations in RNA synthesis, and affect physiology and differentiation decisions in otherwise identical cells.
evidence: This is a general statement about transcription that draws from established scientific understanding of the process.

claim: Fluctuations at every step of transcription can cause variations in RNA synthesis.
source: Transcription is an inherently stochastic, noisy, and multi-step process, in which fluctuations at every step can cause variations in RNA synthesis, and affect physiology and differentiation decisions in otherwise identical cells.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about transcriptional variability.

claim: Fluctuations in transcription can affect physiology and differentiation decisions in otherwise identical cells.
source: Transcription is an inherently stochastic, noisy, and multi-step process, in which fluctuations at every step can cause variations in RNA synthesis, and affect physiology and differentiation decisions in otherwise identical cells.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about the biological consequences of transcriptional variability.

claim: FastFISH achieves exceptionally fast rates of specific hybridization (∼10e7 M−1s−1).
source: Here we established a fast fluorescence in situ hybridization (fastFISH) method that takes advantage of intrinsically unstructured nucleic acid sequences to achieve exceptionally fast rates of specific hybridization (∼10e7 M−1s−1), and allows deterministic detection of single nascent transcripts.
evidence: The hybridization rate is measured experimentally as shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: FastFISH allows deterministic detection of single nascent transcripts.
source: Here we established a fast fluorescence in situ hybridization (fastFISH) method that takes advantage of intrinsically unstructured nucleic acid sequences to achieve exceptionally fast rates of specific hybridization (∼10e7 M−1s−1), and allows deterministic detection of single nascent transcripts.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figures 2 and 4.

claim: FastFISH takes advantage of intrinsically unstructured nucleic acid sequences.
source: Here we established a fast fluorescence in situ hybridization (fastFISH) method that takes advantage of intrinsically unstructured nucleic acid sequences to achieve exceptionally fast rates of specific hybridization (∼10e7 M−1s−1), and allows deterministic detection of single nascent transcripts.
evidence: This design principle is described and tested in Figure 1.

claim: FastFISH can measure the kinetic rates of promoter escape, elongation, and termination at the single-molecule level at sub-second temporal resolution.
source: Using a prototypical RNA polymerase, we demonstrated the use of fastFISH to measure the kinetic rates of promoter escape, elongation, and termination in one assay at the single-molecule level, at sub-second temporal resolution.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figures 3, 4, and 5.

claim: RNA polymerase binds to the promoter to form the closed complex (RPc).
source: Transcription is a dynamic, multi-step process in which RNA polymerase (RNAP) (i) binds to the promoter to form the closed complex (RPc); (ii) melts the promoter to form the open complex (RPo); (iii) performs several abortive cycles of synthesis and release of short 2–12 nt RNA products as the initial transcribing complex (RPitc); (iv) escapes the promoter; (v) undergoes some promoter-proximal pausing; (vi) forms an elongating complex (RDe) whose processivity can either be interrupted by more pauses or stimulated by trailing RNAPs and elongation factors; and, finally (vii) terminates at the end of the transcription unit (reviewed in DeHaseth et al., 1998; Murakami and Darst, 2003; Cheung and Cramer, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: RNA polymerase melts the promoter to form the open complex (RPo).
source: Transcription is a dynamic, multi-step process in which RNA polymerase (RNAP) (i) binds to the promoter to form the closed complex (RPc); (ii) melts the promoter to form the open complex (RPo); (iii) performs several abortive cycles of synthesis and release of short 2–12 nt RNA products as the initial transcribing complex (RPitc); (iv) escapes the promoter; (v) undergoes some promoter-proximal pausing; (vi) forms an elongating complex (RDe) whose processivity can either be interrupted by more pauses or stimulated by trailing RNAPs and elongation factors; and, finally (vii) terminates at the end of the transcription unit (reviewed in DeHaseth et al., 1998; Murakami and Darst, 2003; Cheung and Cramer, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: RNA polymerase performs several abortive cycles of synthesis and release of short 2–12 nt RNA products as the initial transcribing complex (RPitc).
source: Transcription is a dynamic, multi-step process in which RNA polymerase (RNAP) (i) binds to the promoter to form the closed complex (RPc); (ii) melts the promoter to form the open complex (RPo); (iii) performs several abortive cycles of synthesis and release of short 2–12 nt RNA products as the initial transcribing complex (RPitc); (iv) escapes the promoter; (v) undergoes some promoter-proximal pausing; (vi) forms an elongating complex (RDe) whose processivity can either be interrupted by more pauses or stimulated by trailing RNAPs and elongation factors; and, finally (vii) terminates at the end of the transcription unit (reviewed in DeHaseth et al., 1998; Murakami and Darst, 2003; Cheung and Cramer, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Molecular fluctuations at any step of transcription may cause large cell-to-cell variability in the amount of the final RNA transcript produced.
source: Due to the low copy number of genes in a cell (usually one in prokaryotes and two in eukaryotes), molecular fluctuations at any of the above steps may cause large cell-to-cell variability in the amount of the final RNA transcript produced in populations of otherwise genetically identical cells grown under identical conditions, and thus can affect gene expression, and cell physiology (Ogawa, 1993; Raj and Van Oudenaarden, 2009; Yamanaka, 2009; Gupta et al., 2011; Lionnet and Singer, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Single-molecule techniques can directly monitor molecular fluctuations in multi-step reactions in real-time without averaging out their inherent stochasticity.
source: Single-molecule techniques are ideally suited to directly monitor molecular fluctuations in multi-step reactions in real-time, without averaging out their inherent stochasticity (Weiss, 1999), and have provided important insights into the dynamics of transcription, unattainable by conventional ensemble methods (Bai et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Single-molecule assays based on optical nanomanipulation have revealed pausing and backtracking of elongating RNA polymerase.
source: For instance, single-molecule assays based on optical nanomanipulation have revealed pausing and backtracking of RDe (Neuman et al., 2003; Shaevitz et al., 2003; Galburt et al., 2007) and measured the force and the torque generated by RDe (Wang et al., 1998; Ma et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Single-molecule assays based on optical nanomanipulation have measured the force and the torque generated by elongating RNA polymerase.
source: For instance, single-molecule assays based on optical nanomanipulation have revealed pausing and backtracking of RDe (Neuman et al., 2003; Shaevitz et al., 2003; Galburt et al., 2007) and measured the force and the torque generated by RDe (Wang et al., 1998; Ma et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Oligonucleotide probes typically hybridize several orders of magnitude slower than diffusion under physiological conditions (effective rate constant kon less than 105 M−1 s−1).
source: However, oligonucleotide probes typically hybridize several orders of magnitude slower than diffusion under physiological conditions (effective rate constant kon less than 105 M−1 s−1, [Chan et al., 1995 and references therein]) and, as a result, do not permit real-time nascent RNA detection with common single-molecule setups, such as total internal reflection fluorescence (TIRF) microscopy.
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: Single-stranded nucleic acid probes with sequences comprised of just three of the four bases (A, U and C for RNA probes, and A, T, and G for the complementary DNA targets) are intrinsically unstructured.
source: The method takes advantage of our finding that single-stranded nucleic acid probes with sequences comprised of just three of the four bases (A, U and C for RNA probes, and A, T, and G for the complementary DNA targets) are intrinsically unstructured and, as a result, hybridize at exceptionally fast rates (∼107 M−1s−1) without compromising sequence specificity.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 1A.

claim: Three-base nucleic acid probes hybridize at exceptionally fast rates (∼107 M−1s−1) without compromising sequence specificity.
source: The method takes advantage of our finding that single-stranded nucleic acid probes with sequences comprised of just three of the four bases (A, U and C for RNA probes, and A, T, and G for the complementary DNA targets) are intrinsically unstructured and, as a result, hybridize at exceptionally fast rates (∼107 M−1s−1) without compromising sequence specificity.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 1C and Figure 1B.

claim: Hybridization of two single-stranded nucleic acid fragments requires unfolding of the fragments into unstructured coils, which then anneal to form an intermolecular base paired helix.
source: Hybridization of two single-stranded nucleic acid fragments requires unfolding of the fragments into unstructured coils, which then anneal to form an intermolecular base paired helix (Lima et al., 1992 and references therein).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: Nucleic acid probes with less stable secondary structures show faster hybridization rates to complementary nucleic acid targets.
source: In support of this notion, nucleic acid probes with less stable secondary structures show faster hybridization rates to complementary nucleic acid targets (Lima et al., 1992; Kushon et al., 2001; Wang and Drlica, 2004; Gao et al., 2006; Yilmaz et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Decreasing the length of hairpins in conventional molecular beacons increases their hybridization rates.
source: Likewise, decreasing the length of hairpins in conventional molecular beacons increases their hybridization rates (Tsourkas et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: An average random 19-mer RNA sequence is mostly structured with ΔG37°C of −1.7 ± 1.7 kCal mol−1.
source: We found that ΔG37°C values were mostly negative and widely distributed (−1.7 ± 1.7 kCal mol−1), indicating that an average random 19-mer RNA sequence is mostly structured (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is based on computational analysis of random sequences using Mfold, as shown in Figure 1A.

claim: 19-mer RNA sequences composed of only A, U, and C have mostly positive ΔG37°C with a much narrower distribution (+2.5 ± 0.6 kCal mol−1).
source: We then calculated ΔG37°C for randomly picked 19-mers composed of only A, U, and C (N = 99,777, GC content between 0.4 and 0.6, Figure 1A), and found that these AUC-sequences had mostly positive ΔG37°C, with a much narrower distribution (+2.5 ± 0.6 kCal mol−1, Figure 1A).
evidence: This is based on computational analysis using Mfold, as shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Mostly unstructured 19-mer RNA sequences with positive ΔG37°C (>+2 kCal mol−1) were composed predominantly of only three bases A, U, and C.
source: Next, we closely examined a subset of 19-mer RNA sequences that had positive ΔG37°C (>+2 kCal mol−1, N = 2,768, <1% of the total pool of random sequences), and found that these mostly unstructured sequences were composed predominantly of only three bases A, U, and C (∼84% had only 2 G residues or less, significantly less than the 4.75 G residues expected on average, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on computational analysis of random sequences, as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Guanine is the most potent in base-pairing interactions because it forms a triple hydrogen bond with cytosine and a wobble pair with uracil.
source: The bias towards the lower G-content in the unstructured sequences was not surprising, because guanine is the most potent in base-paring interactions: it forms a triple hydrogen bond with cytosine and a wobble pair with uracil.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of nucleic acid chemistry.

claim: AUC-sequences were unique among three-base-derived RNA sequences in their largely positive ΔG37°C.
source: Analysis of other three-base-derived RNA sequences (AUG, CAG, CUG) indicated that AUC-sequences were unique in their largely positive ΔG37°C (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is based on computational analysis using Mfold, as shown in Figure 1A.

claim: ATG-based and ATC-based DNA 19-mers are significantly less structured than their four-base counterparts.
source: Calculation of ΔG37°C for random DNA 19-mers (that could be used as complementary probes for RNA targets) indicated that ATG-based and ATC-based DNA 19-mers were also significantly less structured than their four-base counterparts (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is based on computational analysis using Mfold, as shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Three-letter 19-mer sequences have complexity indices of 8.1 ± 0.8.
source: We found that three-letter 19-mer sequences had complexity indices of 8.1 ± 0.8 (N = 99,777), while four-letter 19-mers had complexity indices of 9.3 ± 0.8 (N = 338,417, Figure 1B).
evidence: This is based on Lempel-Ziv complexity analysis, as shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Four-letter 19-mers have complexity indices of 9.3 ± 0.8.
source: We found that three-letter 19-mer sequences had complexity indices of 8.1 ± 0.8 (N = 99,777), while four-letter 19-mers had complexity indices of 9.3 ± 0.8 (N = 338,417, Figure 1B).
evidence: This is based on Lempel-Ziv complexity analysis, as shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Tiling 19-mers in all exons of human chromosome 22 have complexity indices of 8.9 ± 1.0.
source: As a comparative reference, we calculated complexity indices for tiling 19-mers in all exons of human chromosome 22 to be 8.9 ± 1.0 (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is based on Lempel-Ziv complexity analysis, as shown in Figure 1B.

claim: A significant fraction of three-letter 19-mers (∼31%) have complexity indices of 9 and higher, which match or exceed the average complexity of human exons.
source: Importantly, a significant fraction of three-letter 19-mers (∼31%) had complexity indices of 9 and higher, which matched or exceeded the average complexity of human exons.
evidence: This is based on Lempel-Ziv complexity analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The F1 probe anneals to its surface-immobilized RNA target at a rate of 6 × 106 M−1s−1.
source: Indeed, the F1 and F2 probes annealed to their surface-immobilized RNA targets at exceptionally fast rates—6 × 106 M−1s−1 and 4 × 106 M−1s−1, respectively, as measured by TIRF-based Colocalization Single-Molecule Spectroscopy (CoSMoS, Friedman et al., 2006) (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is measured experimentally using TIRF/CoSMoS, as shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The F2 probe anneals to its surface-immobilized RNA target at a rate of 4 × 106 M−1s−1.
source: Indeed, the F1 and F2 probes annealed to their surface-immobilized RNA targets at exceptionally fast rates—6 × 106 M−1s−1 and 4 × 106 M−1s−1, respectively, as measured by TIRF-based Colocalization Single-Molecule Spectroscopy (CoSMoS, Friedman et al., 2006) (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is measured experimentally using TIRF/CoSMoS, as shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The on-rates of F1 and F2 probes are at least 100-fold faster than typical four-base nucleic acid probes of similar lengths reported in literature.
source: These on-rates were at least 100-fold faster than typical four-base nucleic acid probes of similar lengths reported in literature (Lima et al., 1992; Kushon et al., 2001; Wang and Drlica, 2004; Friedman et al., 2006; Gao et al., 2006; Yilmaz et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a comparison to rates reported in cited literature.

claim: Introducing one or more G residues into the F2 RNA target sequence decreases the rate of its hybridization to the complementary DNA probe.
source: Consistent with the AUC rule, introducing back one or more G residues into the F2 RNA target sequence decreased the rate of its hybridization to the complementary DNA probe (10-fold reduction for one G residue and 300-fold reduction for four G residues), which correlated with the progressively lower free energies of self-folding (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is measured experimentally, as shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Introducing one G residue into the F2 RNA target sequence causes a 10-fold reduction in hybridization rate.
source: Consistent with the AUC rule, introducing back one or more G residues into the F2 RNA target sequence decreased the rate of its hybridization to the complementary DNA probe (10-fold reduction for one G residue and 300-fold reduction for four G residues), which correlated with the progressively lower free energies of self-folding (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is measured experimentally, as shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Introducing four G residues into the F2 RNA target sequence causes a 300-fold reduction in hybridization rate.
source: Consistent with the AUC rule, introducing back one or more G residues into the F2 RNA target sequence decreased the rate of its hybridization to the complementary DNA probe (10-fold reduction for one G residue and 300-fold reduction for four G residues), which correlated with the progressively lower free energies of self-folding (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is measured experimentally, as shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Self-quenching of fastFISH probes enables the use of free probes at concentrations up to 1 μM.
source: This self-quenching strategy enabled the use of free probes at concentrations up to 1 μM (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Self-quenching of fastFISH probes is likely mediated by random polymer motion and/or contact quenching.
source: We believe that, in the absence of the secondary structure, the self-quenching effect was likely mediated by random polymer motion and/or contact quenching (Johansson et al., 2002; Marras et al., 2002).
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of secondary structure and citations to relevant literature.

claim: T7 RNAP initiates transcripts at an effective rate of at least 1 s−1 at physiological temperature (37°C).
source: This single-subunit RNAP is an excellent test case for fastFISH: at physiological temperature (37°C) it initiates transcripts at an effective rate of at least 1 s−1 (Martin and Coleman, 1987), and elongates transcripts at ∼240 nt s−1 (Golomb and Chamberlin, 1974; Bonner et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: T7 RNAP elongates transcripts at ∼240 nt s−1.
source: This single-subunit RNAP is an excellent test case for fastFISH: at physiological temperature (37°C) it initiates transcripts at an effective rate of at least 1 s−1 (Martin and Coleman, 1987), and elongates transcripts at ∼240 nt s−1 (Golomb and Chamberlin, 1974; Bonner et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Specific probe-DNA interactions were observed with wild type promoter templates but not with null mutant promoter templates.
source: Specific probe-DNA interactions were observed, as indicated by a prominent peak at position (0, 0) of the co-localization histogram. In a typical experiment, 10–30% of DNA templates in a field of view co-localized with a probe. This apparent incomplete template utilization was not due to inefficient probe hybridization (see Figure 4 and 'Discussion'), but, instead, was likely limited by the accessibility of the DNA template due to surface interference. No probe-DNA interactions were observed in a control experiment with a DNA template containing a null mutant promoter (Raskin et al., 1993), indicating that the co-localization was due to promoter-specific transcription.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 2B and 2D.

claim: 10–30% of DNA templates in a field of view co-localized with a probe in typical fastFISH experiments.
source: In a typical experiment, 10–30% of DNA templates in a field of view co-localized with a probe.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations.

claim: Incomplete template utilization in fastFISH experiments was likely limited by the accessibility of the DNA template due to surface interference, not inefficient probe hybridization.
source: This apparent incomplete template utilization was not due to inefficient probe hybridization (see Figure 4 and 'Discussion'), but, instead, was likely limited by the accessibility of the DNA template due to surface interference.
evidence: This is an inference based on the high efficiency of RNA detection shown in Figure 4.

claim: RNAP-DNA binding events were comprised of two distinct populations: short-lived events with mean dwell time T0 ∼0.14 s and long-lived events with peak dwell time T1 ∼1.7 s.
source: We observed transient RNAP binding events that lasted between 0.08 and 8 s, and were promoter-specific (Figure 3B–D). The events were comprised of two distinct populations: short-lived events whose dwell times fit well to a single exponential distribution (mean dwell time T0 ∼0.14 s); and a long-lived, bell-shaped population skewed towards long-lived events (peak dwell time T1 ∼1.7 s).
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Short-lived RNAP-DNA interactions are promoter-specific but non-productive RPc and RPo.
source: We interpret the short-lived, stochastic interactions to be promoter-specific but non-productive RPc and RPo, because no interactions were observed with templates containing a null promoter sequence (at frame rates of 12.5 Hz, Figure 3B) and similar short-lived interactions were observed in the absence of NTPs (single exponential T0 ∼0.3 s, Figure 3D).
evidence: This interpretation is based on experimental observations with null promoter and absence of NTPs, as shown in Figure 3B and 3D.

claim: Long-lived RNAP-DNA interactions represent full, productive transcription cycles.
source: We interpret the long-lived, bell-shaped population of events to be full, productive transcription cycles, because (i) the long-lived events were not observed in the absence of NTPs (Figure 3D); (ii) the peak dwell time of the long-lived events, T1, increased nearly linearly with the length of the transcribed DNA segment (T1 ∼1.7 s, ∼2.7 s, and ∼3.7 s for DNA segments with l = 295 bp, 633 bp, and 910 bp, respectively, Figure 3E–G); and (iii) the RNAP fluorescence signal, on average, decayed towards the end of long-lived events (Figure 3C,H), consistent with RNAP initiating transcription at the promoter located close to the surface (75 bp, or ∼25 nm), and then elongating towards the free, untethered DNA end, down the gradient of the TIRF evanescent field.
evidence: This interpretation is based on multiple experimental observations shown in Figures 3C, 3D, 3E-G, and 3H.

claim: The peak dwell time of long-lived RNAP-DNA events increases nearly linearly with the length of the transcribed DNA segment (T1 ∼1.7 s for 295 bp, ∼2.7 s for 633 bp, and ∼3.7 s for 910 bp).
source: the peak dwell time of the long-lived events, T1, increased nearly linearly with the length of the transcribed DNA segment (T1 ∼1.7 s, ∼2.7 s, and ∼3.7 s for DNA segments with l = 295 bp, 633 bp, and 910 bp, respectively, Figure 3E–G)
evidence: This is measured experimentally, as shown in Figure 3E-G.

claim: The slope of the plot of long-lived RNAP dwell times vs DNA length gives an estimate of RNAP elongation rate of ∼300 nt s−1.
source: We note that the slope of the plot of long-lived RNAP dwell times vs DNA length, (∼3.2 ± 0.6) × 10−3 s nt−1 (Figure 3G), gives an estimate of RNAP elongation rate of ∼300 nt s−1.
evidence: This is calculated from experimental data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The intercept of the plot of RNAP dwell times vs DNA length gives an estimate of the net time that RNAP spends on the DNA template without elongating, Tstationary = 0.7 ± 0.3 s.
source: The intercept of the plot with the time axis (l = 0) gives an estimate of the net time that RNAP spends on the DNA template without elongating, Tstationary = 0.7 ± 0.3 s, which includes the net duration of promoter opening and abortive cycling (RPc, RPo and RPits), and, possibly, the time RNAP idles at the free DNA end before run-off.
evidence: This is calculated from experimental data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The probe arrived at the DNA within 1 s after arrival of RNAP in typical transcription events.
source: Typically, the probe arrived at the DNA within 1 s after arrival of RNAP.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: No binding of F1 probe after RNAP binding was observed in the presence of only ATP and GTP, which limited initial transcription to positions from +1 to +6.
source: First, no binding of F1 after RNAP binding was observed in the absence of NTPs (data not shown), or in the presence of only ATP and GTP, which limited initial transcription to positions from +1 to +6 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), indicating that the probe bound specifically to the nascent RNA, and not to RNAP or to the DNA template.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: No F1 probe binding was observed in the absence of the target sequence in the transcribed segment of the template.
source: Second, no F1 probe binding was observed in the absence of the target sequence in the transcribed segment of the template, indicating that hybridization was specific for the F1 target (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: When the F1 target sequence was moved from position +28 to position +181, binding of the probe was delayed by an additional ∼0.5 s.
source: Third, and most importantly, when we moved the F1 target sequence from position +28 to position +181, we found that binding of the probe was delayed by an additional ∼0.5 s (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), consistent with the extra time RDe needs to transcribe the extra 153 bp DNA segment at 300 nt s−1 (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: ∼81% of elongating RNAP complexes contained an RNA probe immediately before run-off.
source: We found that ∼81% of RDes contained an RNA probe immediately before run-off (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is measured experimentally, as shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The residual ∼19% of undetected elongating RNAP complexes were mostly likely due to the presence of dark fluorophores in the chemically synthesized probes and the inherent stochasticity of probe hybridization.
source: The residual ∼19% of undetected RDes were mostly likely due to the presence of dark fluorophores in the chemically synthesized probes (Revyakin et al., 2012), and the inherent stochasticity of probe hybridization.
evidence: This is an inference based on known properties of fluorophores and hybridization kinetics, with a citation.

claim: In the majority of cases (∼72%), the probe and RNAP dissociated from the DNA simultaneously upon run-off (ΔToff ∼0).
source: The heat map analysis of all RNAP-DNA and probe-DNA interactions also showed that, in the majority of cases (∼72%), the probe and RNAP dissociated from the DNA simultaneously upon run-off (ΔToff ∼0).
evidence: This is measured experimentally, as shown in Figure 4E and 4F.

claim: In ∼28% of cases, the RNA probe persisted on the DNA for ≥0.4 s after RNAP run-off.
source: In the remaining ∼28% of cases, the RNA probe persisted on the DNA for ≥0.4 s after RNAP run-off (Figure 4F); the nature of these events remains to be determined.
evidence: This is measured experimentally, as shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The average time delay between RNAP and probe arrival (ΔTon) is 0.7 ± 0.2 s.
source: Analysis of the resulting heat-map of probe and RNAP binding gave the average time delay between the RNAP and probe arrival, ΔTon of 0.7 ± 0.2 s.
evidence: This is measured experimentally, as shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The net duration of abortive cycling (Tabortive) is ∼0.2 s.
evidence: This is calculated from experimental measurements of ΔTon, elongation rate, and probe hybridization rate.

claim: RNAP might dwell at the end of the DNA template for ∼0.5 s before run-off.
source: The fact that Tstationary is larger than Tabortive, suggests that RNAP might dwell at the end of the DNA template for ∼0.5 s before run-off.
evidence: This is inferred from the difference between Tstationary and Tabortive.

claim: The hybridization rates of fastFISH probes exceeded annealing rates of probe-target sequences reported in literature by up to three orders of magnitude.
source: The hybridization rates of fastFISH probes were near ∼107 M−1s−1 which exceeded annealing rates of probe-target sequences reported in literature by up to three orders of magnitude.
evidence: This is a comparison to rates reported in literature, based on experimental measurements in Figure 1C.

claim: The three-base rule of fast hybridization also applies to DNA–DNA pairs.
source: We note that the three-base rule of fast hybridization also applies to DNA–DNA pairs (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from unpublished data.

claim: Self-quenching of fastFISH probes likely occurs through random polymer motion and/or contact quenching and does not rely on hairpin formation.
source: Self-quenching of fastFISH probes likely occurs through random polymer motion and/or contact quenching (Johansson et al., 2002; Marras et al., 2002), and does not rely on hairpin formation (which is known to compromise hybridization rates [Tsourkas et al., 2003]).
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of secondary structure and citations to relevant literature.

claim: The measured rate of stochastic RPc dissociation (T0 ∼0.3 s, koff ∼3 s−1) was higher than what had been reported in previous ensemble and single-molecule studies (koff from 0.4 s−1 to 1 s−1).
source: First, the measured rate of stochastic RPc dissociation (T0 ∼0.3 s, koff ∼3 s−1) was higher than what had been reported in previous ensemble and single-molecule studies (koff from 0.4 s−1 to 1 s−1 [Tang and Patel, 2006; Tang et al., 2009]).
evidence: This is a comparison of experimental measurements to previous studies cited.

claim: The measured rate of promoter escape (Tabortive ∼0.2 s, kescape ∼5 s−1) was higher than in previous ensemble and single-molecule studies (kescape from 0.25 s−1 to 1 s−1).
source: Second, the measured rate of promoter escape (Tabortive ∼0.2 s, kescape ∼5 s−1) was higher than in previous ensemble and single-molecule studies (kescape from 0.25 s−1 to 1 s−1, [Skinner et al., 2004; Tang et al., 2009]).
evidence: This is a comparison of experimental measurements to previous studies cited.

claim: The measured peak elongation rate (300 ± 60 nt s−1) was somewhat higher than in previous ensemble measurements (∼240 nt s−1) and significantly higher than in previous single-molecule measurements (from 40 nt s−1 to 120 nt s−1).
source: Third, the measured peak elongation rate (300 ± 60 nt s−1) was somewhat higher than in previous ensemble measurements (∼240 nt s−1, Bonner et al., 1994; Golomb and Chamberlin, 1974), and significantly higher than in previous single-molecule measurements (from 40 nt s−1 to 120 nt s−1, Thomen et al., 2008; Skinner et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a comparison of experimental measurements to previous studies cited.

claim: The overall faster rates measured in this study are likely due to the use of optimal physiological temperatures (37°C).
source: The overall faster rates measured in our study are likely due to the use of optimal physiological temperatures (37°C). Indeed, the catalytic rate of the T7 RNAP measured in steady-state conditions is known to increase up to 10-fold in the 20°C–37°C temperature range (Maslak and Martin, 1993).
evidence: This is an inference supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The dwell time distribution of productive RNAP-DNA interactions was skewed towards longer-lasting events, likely due to spontaneous RNAP pausing.
source: We note that the dwell time distribution of productive RNAP-DNA interactions was skewed towards longer-lasting events, likely due to spontaneous RNAP pausing.
